metadata.title: Context-aware prompting for collaborative problem solving skill identification

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses two experimental CPS task datasets (Three-Resistor and Mondrian Geometric Fantasy) collected from university/community-college students in the United States and high-school students in China, respectively, rather than an ILSA microdata release with official sampling weights. The methodology describes stratified sampling for train/validation/test splits (7:1.5:1.5) but does not report applying any complex survey weights or replicate-weight procedures. Because the models are text/sequence classifiers trained with BERT-based architectures, the manuscript does not discuss weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) and there is no indication that population-representative weighting was used. Therefore, results should be interpreted as task-dataset performance under the experimental sampling scheme, not as weighted estimates of national CPS skill distributions.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not analyze ILSA cognitive achievement scores with Plausible Values; instead, it predicts CPS skill labels from chat messages in two experimental CPS tasks. Missing-data handling is not described as a formal imputation/deletion protocol for the analytic modeling stage; the only explicit exclusions are dataset-level removals of invalid team samples in the Mondrian dataset due to disconnections and missing data. As a result, the missing-data strategy for model training/validation/test construction is not fully transparent, which limits reproducibility regarding how incomplete dialogues were treated beyond the stated exclusions.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Three-Resistor (Dataset 1): 378 university/community-college students in the United States participated; participants were randomly assigned to 126 teams of three, with seating separation and anonymous virtual usernames. The dataset was preprocessed by removing blank chat entries and invalid labels, and by anonymizing/removing personally identifiable information while retaining group identifiers and behavioral logs; the final dataset comprised 34,851 manipulation entries and 15,895 chat entries. Mondrian Geometric Fantasy (Dataset 2): 840 Grade 10–11 students in China formed 280 teams; 51 teams were excluded as invalid due to unexpected disconnections and missing data, leaving 229 valid team samples. For modeling, the study further restricted to chat entries from the formal task phase with blank chat removed, yielding 216,547 manipulation entries and 26,715 chat entries. For both datasets, the chat-message CPS coding task was trained using stratified sampling to split data into training/validation/test sets with a 7:1.5:1.5 ratio.

main_findings.dataset_used: Three-Resistor CPS task (PISA 2015-aligned skill matrix), university/community-college students, chat-message CPS skill coding
main_findings.performance_metrics: CAP4CPS: Accuracy 81.04±0.54; Weighted-F1 80.78±0.55; Cohen’s Kappa 75.33±0.72. Best baseline comparison: BERT-finetune Accuracy 80.24±0.49; Weighted-F1 80.13±0.51; Kappa 74.44±0.64. Ablation: w/o Context Kappa 74.96±0.74; w/o Attention Kappa 75.22±0.80; w/o All Kappa 74.90±0.69.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Three-Resistor CPS task data (PISA 2015-aligned skill matrix) for chat-message CPS skill coding, the study leveraged cognitive context window, social context window, skill class imbalance, and chat message length to predict CPS skill labels, finding that CAP4CPS achieved the highest Accuracy (81.04%), Weighted-F1 (80.78%), and Cohen’s Kappa (75.33) across models. This indicates that context-aware, multi-dimensional prompting with attention-based fusion can improve automated CPS skill coding accuracy, supporting more scalable and potentially near-real-time CPS assessment pipelines, though the results are based on experimental datasets and do not establish causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: Mondrian Geometric Fantasy CPS task (PISA 2015-aligned skill framework), Grade 10–11 students, chat-message CPS skill coding
main_findings.performance_metrics: CAP4CPS: Accuracy 83.27±0.36; Weighted-F1 83.17±0.38; Cohen’s Kappa 78.37±0.48. Best baseline comparison: BERT-seq Accuracy 82.70±0.64; Weighted-F1 82.65±0.58; Kappa 77.63±0.76. Ablation: w/o Context Kappa 77.07±0.85; w/o Attention Kappa 78.36±0.56; w/o All Kappa 76.99±0.74.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Mondrian Geometric Fantasy CPS task data (PISA 2015-aligned skill framework) for chat-message CPS skill coding, the study leveraged cognitive context window, social context window, skill class imbalance, and chat message length to predict CPS skill labels, finding that CAP4CPS achieved the highest Accuracy (83.27%), Weighted-F1 (83.17%), and Cohen’s Kappa (78.37) among compared models. This indicates that explicitly modeling contextual dependencies in prompts and fusing cognitive/social representations improves automated CPS skill identification, which can inform the design of automated coding tools for large-scale CSCL/CPS data, while generalizability remains limited to the two evaluated tasks and no survey-weighted population inference is possible.

data.outcome_summary: The study proposes CAP4CPS, a context-aware prompting framework for automated collaborative problem solving (CPS) skill coding from chat-message process data. It evaluates the approach on two experimental CPS datasets: Three-Resistor (378 U.S. university/community-college students) and Mondrian Geometric Fantasy (840 Chinese Grade 10–11 students; 51 teams excluded as invalid, leaving 229 valid teams). CAP4CPS uses BERT-based prompt embeddings with separate cognitive and social context extraction (historical dialogue windows) and an attention-based fusion module to predict CPS subskill labels. Across both datasets, CAP4CPS outperforms strong baselines, reaching Accuracy 81.04%/83.27%, Weighted-F1 80.78/83.17, and Cohen’s Kappa 75.33/78.37 (Three-Resistor/Mondrian). The paper reports stratified train/validation/test splits but does not provide a formal missing-data handling protocol beyond dataset-level exclusions, and it does not use ILSA PVs or survey weights, so results reflect task-dataset classification performance rather than population-representative achievement estimates.
